fields.Back: How closely related the functions and responsibilities within a single module are; the degree to which elements inside a module belong together.
The degree of dependency between modules; how closely two classes or components are connected.

fields.Front: Is high or low cohesion desirable? Is high or low coupling desirable?

fields.Text: High cohesion follows the {{c1::Single Responsibility Principle}}; low coupling follows the {{c2::Dependency Inversion Principle}}.

fields.Front: Give the slide's example of a highly cohesive class.
fields.Back: ShoppingCart whose methods addItem(), removeItem(), calculateTotal() are all about managing the cart.

fields.Front: What are the consequences of low cohesion?
fields.Back: Responsibilities are spread across unrelated tasks; modules are harder to maintain; changing one part can inadvertently affect unrelated parts.

fields.Text: High cohesion matters for ease of {{c1::understanding}}, ease of {{c2::maintenance}}, and {{c3::reusability}}.
Low coupling matters for ease of {{c1::maintenance}}, {{c2::flexibility}}, and {{c3::testing}}.
The ideal design scenario is {{c1::high cohesion}} + {{c2::low coupling}}.

fields.Back: Modules are internally well-organized but have strong dependencies on other modules.
Modules are independent, but poorly organized internally.
Modules are disorganized internally and highly dependent on others (the worst case).

fields.Text: {{c1::Cohesion}} measures how well elements inside one module belong together; {{c2::coupling}} measures dependency between modules.
Low coupling means changes in one module have {{c1::minimal impact}} on others.
